subtype: Boss expects excellence or expects nothing [Receiver]
passage: The monsoon had flooded the office basement, so the interns worked from the cramped meeting room with a leaking ceiling and a deadline on Friday. Their manager, Mr Rao, had decided on day one that Yusuf was "the sharp one." He gave Yusuf the client analysis, sat with him over drafts, and said, "Push harder, I know you can." Minakshi got photocopying and meeting notes. Nobody read her notes. Nobody told her what was good or bad. By the third week, Yusuf was presenting to clients. Minakshi was finishing early and scrolling her phone, not because she was lazy, but because nothing she did seemed to matter. On Friday, as buckets filled under the drips, she wondered if she was the dull one after all.

qa.q: What did Mr Rao give Yusuf to work on?
qa.a: The client analysis.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling by the third week?
qa.a: She felt ignored and discouraged, starting to doubt her own ability because nothing she did seemed to matter.

qa.q: What could Mr Rao do to give Minakshi a fair chance?
qa.a: Give her a real task with honest feedback, as he did for Yusuf, and judge her by the results.

qa.q: How might Yusuf be affected by Mr Rao's high expectations?
qa.a: Yusuf likely feels challenged and confident, rising to the stretch work and presenting to clients.

grounding: Illustrates how an intern expected to excel receives stretch tasks and feedback while another treated as filler coasts.

passage: In the hotel's front-office team, Nirmala had been manager for six months. One Monday, updating the roster, she noticed a pattern. Every tricky guest complaint went to Sameer. Every routine check-in went to Arohi. She tried to remember why. Arohi had once fumbled a phone call in her first week. That was it. One call. Nirmala felt a flush of discomfort. She changed the roster. That week, Arohi handled a double-booking dispute. Nirmala sat nearby, gave her the same notes she gave Sameer, and waited patiently when Arohi paused. Arohi solved it well, with a calm apology and a free breakfast offer. Nirmala wrote it down. From then on, she rotated the hard cases and judged by what actually happened.

qa.q: What did Arohi handle in the new roster week?
qa.a: A double-booking dispute.

qa.q: What did Nirmala feel when she remembered why Arohi got routine tasks?
qa.a: She felt a flush of discomfort, realising one fumbled call in the first week had shaped months of expectations.

qa.q: What steps did Nirmala take to check her own expectations?
qa.a: She rotated the hard cases, gave Arohi the same notes and patience as Sameer, and recorded actual results.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel being given the double-booking dispute?
qa.a: Arohi might feel nervous but trusted, and proud after solving it well.

grounding: Shows a manager noticing she gives tough work to one person and routine to another, then equalising challenge and judging by evidence.

subtype: Parent who is sure of what the child is [Actor]
passage:
Madhuri: diwali party at your cousin's tonight. i'll handle the aunties so Pihu doesn't have to talk
Lalit: she's 5, she can say hello 🙂
Madhuri: u know she's the shy one
Lalit: she sang to the whole building at the dussehra function
Madhuri: that was different
Lalit: last time aunty asked her name and u answered before she opened her mouth
Madhuri: bcoz she'd freeze
Lalit: maybe she freezes bcoz we always answer for her
Madhuri: ...
Madhuri: that stings a bit
Lalit: i'm not blaming u. i do it too
Madhuri: ok. tonight i'll wait. count to five before i jump in
Lalit: deal. let's see what she does
Madhuri: if she hides behind me, i'll let her 🙂

qa.q: When did Pihu sing to the whole building?
qa.a: At the Dussehra function.

qa.q: How does Madhuri feel when Lalit suggests Pihu freezes because they answer for her?

qa.q: What is Madhuri's plan for the party, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To count to five before answering for Pihu, which gives Pihu room to speak and grow.

qa.q: How might Pihu be affected if her parents always answer for her?
qa.a: Pihu might start to believe she is the shy one and stop trying to speak for herself.

grounding: Illustrates a parent convinced her child is shy and answering for her, and how expecting growth gives the child room.

subtype: Small treat seems big or small by comparison [Actor]
passage: At the winter fair in the village, the sweet-seller gave Disha a plain round biscuit. "Thank you!" She nibbled it happily. Then he gave her one with a sugar flower on top. "Ooh!" Disha beamed. It was the best biscuit ever. Then her big brother Kishore came back from the other stall with a huge chocolate one. Disha looked at her flower biscuit. Her lip wobbled. "His is bigger." Her flower biscuit hadn't changed at all. Maa squeezed her hand. "Yours has a flower. His doesn't." Disha looked again, and sniffed.

qa.q: What was on top of Disha's second biscuit?
qa.a: A sugar flower.

qa.q: Why did Disha's lip wobble when Kishore came back?
qa.a: She felt sad and disappointed, because next to his huge chocolate biscuit her flower biscuit suddenly seemed small.

qa.q: What did Maa do to help Disha see her biscuit differently?
qa.a: She pointed out that Disha's biscuit had a flower and Kishore's didn't, giving her a new thing to compare.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel seeing Disha upset?
qa.a: Kishore might feel a little awkward or proud, not realising his big biscuit made hers look small.

grounding: Shows a young child whose happiness with a biscuit changes depending on what it is compared with.

passage: Christmas-week report cards were handed out in the school hall, under paper stars. Lavanya opened hers: sixty-eight in science. Not bad, she thought. Then Pooja squealed beside her. "Ninety-six!" Lavanya's sixty-eight suddenly looked tiny. She folded the card and felt her throat tighten. She hardly spoke on the way back to class. Then Sir said, "This test was tough. Class average was fifty-four." Lavanya unfolded her card. Sixty-eight. Fourteen above average! She grinned all afternoon. At home, she told Amma, "I did really well!" Amma asked, "Better than this morning?" Lavanya paused. "It's the same mark," she admitted, laughing. "It just feels different."

qa.q: What was the class average?
qa.a: Fifty-four.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel when Pooja squealed "Ninety-six"?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and small, her own mark suddenly seeming tiny.

qa.q: What could Lavanya compare her mark with to judge it fairly?
qa.a: Her own past marks or how much she improved, rather than just the nearest friend's score.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel if she saw Lavanya's mood drop?
qa.a: Pooja might feel a bit awkward, not meaning her excitement to make Lavanya feel worse.

grounding: Illustrates a student whose feelings about the same mark change with the reference point.

subtype: Feeling plain after scrolling edited photos [Actor]
passage: On summer holiday afternoons in the small town, with the power cutting in and out, Ojas lay on the charpoy and scrolled. Face after face: clear skin, perfect jaws, soft light. An hour later, he got up and looked in the steel mirror by the water pot. His nose looked too big. His skin looked bumpy. He felt plain and ugly. The next morning, at the tuition class, he sat with Tenzin and the others. There were pimples and sunburn and messy hair everywhere. Tenzin had a scratch from a cricket ball. Ojas looked around. Everyone looked normal. He looked normal. His face hadn't changed overnight. Only what he'd been looking at had.

qa.q: Where did Ojas look at himself after scrolling?
qa.a: In the steel mirror by the water pot.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel after an hour of scrolling?
qa.a: He felt plain and ugly, unhappy with his nose and skin after comparing himself with polished photos.

qa.q: What could Ojas do to protect how he feels about himself?
qa.a: He could limit scrolling polished photos and remember that real faces, like at tuition, are the fair comparison.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see Ojas that morning?
qa.a: Tenzin probably sees an ordinary friend, with no idea Ojas felt ugly the day before.

grounding: Shows a teenager feeling unattractive after scrolling edited photos and normal again among real classmates.

subtype: Bargain looks cheap next to a costly item [Observer]
passage: "Tushar, look at this jacket." Jomon held up the leather one, the price tag nearly five figures. "Too much." "Way too much," Tushar agreed. They walked to the next rack. Jomon picked up a shirt. "Okay, this is only two thousand. That's cheap!" "Is it?" "Compared to the jacket!" "Jomon, last month you said a shirt over eight hundred was a rip-off." Jomon paused. "That was different." "Was it? It's the same shirt money." Jomon looked at the tag again. "Huh. It just felt cheap after the jacket." "That's what they want," Tushar said. "They put the jacket first." Jomon put the shirt back, then picked it up again. "I still like it, though." "Then decide on the shirt, not the jacket."

qa.q: What did Jomon say about shirts last month?
qa.a: That a shirt over eight hundred was a rip-off.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when calling the shirt cheap?
qa.a: Jomon felt pleased and relieved, sure of a bargain because the jacket made the shirt seem cheap.

qa.q: What does Tushar suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To decide on the shirt by itself, not against the jacket, so the last thing seen doesn't set the judgment.

qa.q: How does Tushar see Jomon's reaction?
qa.a: Tushar sees that Jomon's judgment followed the expensive jacket, and notices the shop's placement.

grounding: Illustrates a friend observing how a costly jacket made a mid-priced shirt seem cheap.

passage:
Dear Sudha,
You asked which flat I picked. I nearly chose the one on the ninth floor. After seeing the tiny, dark one first, it looked like a palace. Then I stopped and asked myself: what is it worth by itself? Is it what I need, compared with where I lived last year and what I actually use? Honestly, no. It was far from my office, and I'd be spending two hours a day in traffic. The second flat I saw was smaller but a ten-minute walk away. I also stopped comparing myself to the friends who post their huge living rooms. Those are their best angles, not their lives. I'm signing for the small one on Monday. I think I'll be happy there.
Afreen

qa.q: How far is the smaller flat from Afreen's office?
qa.a: A ten-minute walk away.

qa.q: How does Afreen seem to feel about the decision?
qa.a: Afreen seems calm, settled and hopeful, confident the small flat will make for a happier life.

qa.q: What questions helped Afreen choose well?
qa.a: Asking what the flat is worth by itself, and comparing it with last year's home and real needs rather than the tiny dark flat or friends' posts.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel reading about Afreen's choice?
qa.a: Sudha might feel glad and reassured that Afreen chose based on real needs.

grounding: Shows an adult choosing the reference point deliberately instead of judging a flat against the nearest example or others' highlights.

subtype: Combo choice pushed by a pointless third option [Actor]
passage: The Christmas-week show started in five minutes, and Lalremsiami and Zainab had only a little pocket money between them. The popcorn board had three options: small for eighty, large for two hundred, and medium for one hundred and ninety. "Medium's almost as much as large," Zainab said. "Then large is a bargain!" said Lalremsiami. "It's only ten more." They bought the large. Inside the dark hall, they ate half and left the rest, too full. Walking out, Lalremsiami looked at the board again. "Wait. Why would anyone ever buy the medium?" Zainab laughed. "Maybe no one's supposed to." Lalremsiami frowned. The large had felt like such a clever choice.

qa.q: How much was the medium popcorn?
qa.a: One hundred and ninety.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel when choosing the large popcorn?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt clever and pleased, sure of spotting a bargain.

qa.q: What could the friends ask themselves next time at the counter?
qa.a: Whether they actually want that much, comparing the small with what they'll eat, not the large with the odd medium.

qa.q: How does Zainab see the medium option by the end?
qa.a: Zainab suspects the medium is there only to make the large look like a bargain.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager choosing the large popcorn because an odd middle option made it seem like good value.

passage: Exam season in the college hostel meant everyone needed the study app. Lavanya sat in the common room with Shankar, comparing plans on her phone. Basic: free, with ads. Standard: two hundred a month, no ads. Premium: two hundred and twenty, no ads, all courses, offline notes. "Premium's obviously better," Lavanya said. "Only twenty more than standard." Shankar leaned over. "Do you even need all courses? You use one." "But it's such good value." She bought premium. A month later, she had opened one course and never used offline notes. Shankar showed her: the basic plan's ads were only on the home screen. Lavanya groaned. The standard plan had been there just to make premium look smart.

qa.q: How much more than standard did premium cost?
qa.a: Twenty more.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel when she chose premium?
qa.a: She felt smart and satisfied, believing she had found the obvious best value.

qa.q: What could Lavanya ask before choosing a plan next time?
qa.a: What she actually needs and uses, instead of comparing premium only with the barely cheaper middle plan.

qa.q: How does Shankar see Lavanya's choice?
qa.a: Shankar is sceptical, asking whether she even needs all courses when she uses one.

grounding: Shows a young adult picking the premium plan because an odd middle option made it look like obvious value.
